claims.claim: A study found that butterfly wings create an optical illusion that allows butterflies to evade predators (מחקר: כנפי הפרפרים יוצרות אשליה אופטית שמאפשרת להם לחמוק מטורפים).
claims.verified_figure: Nature paper (Exeter & Essex, 2026-09-30): wing deformation in flight makes stripes act like a barber-pole illusion, generating false motion cues. Evidence: (1) high-speed (>1,000 fps) take-off footage of real butterflies run through a bird-vision motion-detection model — patterned wings produced more misleading motion signals than digitally pattern-removed versions; footage covered only 7 pattern types, 2-3 individuals each; (2) simulation over ~400 European species (dorsal side only, single overhead angle) found illusion-generating patterns widespread; (3) 100 human volunteers, ~3,000 trials on a 240 Hz touchscreen, targets slowed for human reaction times — people struck further behind butterflies whose patterns were predicted to cause more motion confusion; (4) ~50,000 digitally 'evolved' patterns converged on natural-like designs. Per reported limitations: no real bird predators were tested; the work shows patterns can mislead a bird-vision motion model and human attackers, not that the illusion protects butterflies from birds in the wild.
claims.article_figure_per_search_snippet: Article body unreachable (EGRESS_BLOCKED + .premium paywall). Search snippet attributed to the Haaretz piece describes the Nature study (Exeter/Essex), 1,000 fps filming, digital pattern removal and the 100-volunteer touchscreen game, and says the illusion 'allows the butterfly to escape or at least avoid serious injury'. Body may carry hedges not visible; verdict is on the headline only.
claims.note: Audited from headline only (body_ok 0). Direction of the finding is correct and the study is real and peer-reviewed (Nature). But the headline states as established fact that the illusion 'allows them to evade predators', while the evidence is a bird-vision computational model plus a human touchscreen proxy with slowed targets; no test with real predators and no field data. The paper's own reported limitations say it does not show protection from birds in the wild. Note the overstatement largely originates upstream: the university press release title is 'Butterflies use optical illusions to dodge predators', and Haaretz's headline mirrors it; more careful outlets (e.g., ZME Science, StudyFinds, TimesLIVE) used 'may'. Not 'misinterpreted' — the mechanism is described correctly; the issue is certainty/real-world scope.
